stories.title: What's happening on James and Kent streets?
stories.summary: The City is renewing aging sewers, watermains, roads and sidewalks. The plan also includes an eastbound contraflow bicycle lane on James Street. The City lists overall completion in spring/summer 2027.
stories.whyItMatters: This is the kind of project that can change your daily route, sidewalk access and how a street works when construction is finished.
stories.nextStep: Read the City's current construction notices for the latest closures and access information. The original design feedback deadline has passed.

stories.title: Three west-end streets are getting a rebuild
stories.summary: The City is replacing aging water and sewer infrastructure and rebuilding road surfaces along Berkley Avenue, Dominion Avenue and Tay Street. Construction began in August 2026, with completion planned for fall 2027.
stories.whyItMatters: Road reconstruction can affect local access while creating opportunities for drainage, sidewalk and traffic-calming improvements.
stories.nextStep: Check the official project page for construction updates. The July–August 2026 public information period has ended.

stories.title: Work is starting around Walkley Road
stories.summary: A City construction notice says work beginning in mid-October 2026 includes a new Airport Parkway off-ramp, a roundabout at Walkley Road and a multi-use pathway connection. Completion is planned for summer 2028.
stories.whyItMatters: Changes here could affect drivers, people using transit, and anyone walking or cycling in the area.
stories.nextStep: Review the City's project notice for anticipated traffic conditions and updated construction timing.

stories.title: Council approved a plan for 401 homes near transit
stories.summary: Council approved plans for a proposed 30-storey mixed-use building north of Queen Mary Street, including 401 homes and ground-floor commercial space.
stories.whyItMatters: New housing near rapid transit can affect the local housing supply, services, pedestrian activity and streetscape. Approval does not mean a building is already constructed.
stories.nextStep: Read the City's council recap. Later project updates would need to be checked separately; this pilot does not claim construction has started.

stories.title: 347 proposed homes in Stittsville: what changed?
stories.summary: Council approved a zoning amendment for a planned subdivision near Mantra Street. The proposal includes 347 homes, while protecting open space along the Carp River. The City says required site work and updated floodplain mapping must happen before construction.
stories.whyItMatters: A zoning decision is one step in a larger process. The conditions attached to an approval matter just as much as the headline.
stories.nextStep: Check the City's council recap and look for later approvals or project updates before treating this as completed housing.

stories.title: Could a Little Italy park get bigger?
stories.summary: Council approved a motion to waive demolition fees related to three homes on Pamilla Street, supporting the next steps of a land exchange that would expand McCann Park.
stories.whyItMatters: The decision could create more public greenspace, but an approved motion and a finished park expansion are not the same thing.
stories.nextStep: Follow the original council update and check for later information about the proposed land exchange.

stories.title: 613flea is back—and it's free to browse
stories.summary: The organizer lists a Friday evening and Saturday market on November 6 and 7, 2026, with vintage finds, art, makers and more. Admission is free; anything you buy is extra.
stories.whyItMatters: Not every way to enjoy your city needs a ticket or a complicated plan.
stories.nextStep: Check 613flea's own site for updated dates and hours before heading out.
stories.imageDescription: Venue photograph: Horticulture Building and Aberdeen Pavilion at Lansdowne Park, 2012. Not a photograph of this market.

stories.title: Another no-admission flea market weekend
stories.summary: 613flea lists another indoor market for November 27 and 28, 2026. The organizer says admission remains free.
stories.whyItMatters: A local event can be an easy doorway into exploring a neighbourhood and supporting independent makers.
stories.nextStep: Reconfirm the schedule on the organizer's website closer to the date.
stories.imageDescription: Venue photograph: Horticulture Building and Aberdeen Pavilion at Lansdowne Park, 2012. Not a photograph of this market.

stories.title: What is happening at your local library?
stories.summary: Ottawa Public Library publishes a searchable calendar of programs and events, including drop-ins and activities across its branches. Some programs require registration or a library card.
stories.whyItMatters: Neighbourhood libraries are civic spaces as well as places to borrow books. Their activities can offer a low-cost way to connect with people nearby.
stories.nextStep: Browse the current program calendar and check registration details for anything you want to attend.
stories.imageDescription: Ottawa Public Library Main Branch, photographed in 2025. Programs and locations vary by branch.

stories.title: What’s happening around Ottawa this week?
stories.summary: Ottawa Tourism’s event calendar covers concerts, festivals, sports, exhibitions, markets and activities across the region. Some are free; others require tickets or admission.
stories.whyItMatters: A city is more than council decisions. Finding things to do helps people connect with their neighbours and discover new parts of Ottawa.
stories.nextStep: Browse events by date and category. Confirm prices, accessibility and event details directly with the organizer.

stories.title: Music, theatre and more at the National Arts Centre
stories.summary: The NAC lists concerts, theatre, dance and exhibitions, including both ticketed events and free programming.
stories.whyItMatters: Knowing what’s on—and what it costs—makes it easier to find an outing that fits your interests and budget.
stories.nextStep: Check the official events calendar, pricing and availability before making plans.

stories.title: Where do I find open City consultations?
stories.summary: The City publishes public engagement projects and opportunities on its official website. This pilot links to that directory rather than claiming any specific feedback form is open today.
stories.whyItMatters: A participation link is only useful if you can tell what it is about and whether there is still time to respond.
stories.nextStep: Browse the City's public engagement pages. Check each project's exact deadline and participation method before submitting feedback.

stories.title: What happened to the Street Seats pilot?
stories.summary: The City says its 2026 Street Seats season has ended. The pilot temporarily changed sections of several downtown streets to create public space.
stories.whyItMatters: A consultation or pilot ending shouldn't make the story disappear. Residents may still want to know what was learned and what happens next.
stories.nextStep: View the official project page for its published information. This pilot does not claim a new feedback form is open.

stories.title: Kent Street design: can I still comment?
stories.summary: The City held a public information session on August 10, 2026, about the Kent Street functional design study. Its published comment deadline was September 4, 2026.
stories.whyItMatters: Showing a closed deadline is part of closing the loop. It also gives residents a clear record of when feedback was invited.
stories.nextStep: Review the presentation and project materials, and look for future City updates rather than treating the old consultation as open.
